title: Representing America with jazz: the band and embassy concerts
summary: Edison names the tour band and says they played short embassy-hall concerts and were treated like VIPs.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Oh, fantastic. That trip -- the interesting part, we were asked by the American government to go over to represent America for the Bicentennial and they couldn't -- you know, when you represent America in the cultural world, it's jazz, it's the only thing that you can represent. What else has America got to offer?
Who else was in that band?
Benny Carter, Gildo Mahon's and Earl Palmer, drummer, and John Williams, bass player with

the Johnny Carson Show. And a girl singer, who I can't think of her name now, but she was a good singer. Benny Carter recommended her, so there's no doubt about when he recommends somebody. They have talent, you know.
Well, what sort of countries did you play? How many -- how big were they?
We would play in the American embassy halls.
You know, and everyday, we'd have a meeting with the ambassador, the leaders of the -- oh, it was just -- we were treated like VIPs, you know, because we went over for the government.
Would you just play for an hour or something?

We would play 45-minute concert and take a little intermission and take another 45 minutes. Very easy. Oh, very easy, but the people absolutely just went wild. Of course, Louie Armstrong and Duke had been going over there for a long time. Louie Armstrong was the first one to start going over. Then from Pakistan, we went to Amman, Jordan, and we had lunch with the late Queen Alia (PHONETIC) and Princess --
